prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "RTX Corp" (ticker RTX). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)

   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))

   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)

   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: RTX is a top-tier incumbent in a mature industry rather than a Rule Breaker leading an emerging one, and its CEO is a professional manager rather than a founder. It does have strong franchises (Patriot, F135, GTF) and decent momentum (+17% over 12 months), but it fits Gardner's approach only weakly.
summaries.buffett: RTX has durable franchises with decades-long aftermarket tails and a simple-to-grasp defense and aerospace story, which Buffett would appreciate. However, ROIC of roughly 9%, $37.4B of debt, a merger-driven goodwill-heavy balance sheet and a trailing P/E near 32 mean it fails his tests on returns and price.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the long-lived switching costs and oligopoly structure in engines and missiles, but would note the GTF powder-metal recall and fixed-price contract charges as ways the business can stumble. A trailing P/E near 32 with only ~20% gross margins leaves little bargain to justify the complexity.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms RTX is a stalwart with a turnaround element as GTF charges fade and margins recover. With a trailing P/E around 32 and forward P/E near 25 against EPS growth guided around 15%, the PEG is well above 1, so the price looks full by his yardstick.
summaries.fisher: RTX invests heavily in new products (GTF Advantage, LTAMDS, SPY-6, hypersonics, counter-drone) and its R&D clearly produces fielded systems with a record $289B backlog. Its margins are modest and management is a professional team from a merged organization, so it fits Fisher's points partly.
summaries.graham: RTX is large and has paid dividends for decades, but it had a net loss in 2020, trades at about 52 times its three-year average EPS and a P/E times P/B near 120. It fails Graham's defensive-investor valuation criteria clearly.
summaries.thiel: RTX holds monopoly-like positions in a few niches (sole F-35 engine, Tomahawk, SM-6) but its core markets are shared oligopolies and its technology is not ten times better than rivals. It is a durable incumbent rather than a Zero-to-One company built on a secret.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for strong growth at a reasonable price and leaders built for durable change; RTX offers ~10% revenue growth and rising defense demand, but its forward P/E near 25 is rich relative to peers like Lockheed (~17x) and its growth is not tied to a platform shift like AI. It is a partial fit.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are accelerating (adjusted EPS guidance raised twice in 2026 to $7.10-7.25) and geopolitical demand for munitions and air defense is a clear catalyst, which suits Druckenmiller's liquidity-and-earnings focus. But the stock has fallen about 18% from its August 2026 high despite beats, and the valuation already embeds much good news.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital, high gross margins and cash conversion; RTX's ~20% gross margin and ~9% ROIC fall short of his quality bar despite decent free cash flow. It does not fit Fundsmith's 'good company' definition well.
summaries.greenblatt: With an earnings yield (EBIT/EV) of only about 3.3% and ROIC near 9%, RTX scores poorly on both legs of the Magic Formula. It would not rank near the top of a Greenblatt screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool needs a great business, great managers and great reinvestment opportunities; RTX's franchises are durable, but its returns are moderate and reinvestment at high rates is limited by defense pricing and capital intensity. It is a partial fit at best.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses in temporary distress bought at deep discounts; RTX did have a fixable GTF setback, but the stock trades at a premium multiple rather than a distressed price. There is little 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' asymmetry at $186.
summaries.wood: RTX is not a pure-play disruptive-innovation company; its work in autonomy, directed energy and hybrid-electric propulsion is a small part of an incumbent defense and aerospace business. It does not fit ARK's framework.
summaries.ackman: Ackman favors simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative companies with dominant positions and high barriers; RTX has barriers and growing free cash flow ($7,940M in 2025), but its predictability is hurt by program charges and its leverage and valuation are not compelling. It is a partial fit.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model rewards companies that pass savings to customers to widen their moat; RTX prices aftermarket parts for margin rather than sharing scale benefits. It does not fit Nomad's approach well.
summaries.valentine: Valentine sought huge, painful markets addressed by technology at the right moment; RTX addresses large and important problems (air travel, missile defense) but as a century-old incumbent rather than a new venture. The framework applies only loosely.
summaries.nash: RTX passes some of Nash's quality checks (secular defense demand, beating estimates, revenue growing faster than expenses, low short interest) but fails key instant kills: debt of $37.4B exceeds cash of $8.3B and operating margin is about 10-12%, far below 20%. His DCF gives roughly $59 per share versus a $186 price, so it does not fit his approach.

momentum.evidence: The stock is up about 17% over 52 weeks to $186.47 (Oct 14, 2026), but has fallen roughly 18% from its August 10, 2026 high of $226.88.

g4.evidence: CEO Chris Calio has delivered strong results and institutions own over 80% of shares, but there is no famous visionary backer or partner beyond standard index and institutional owners.

g6.evidence: Some commentators note RTX's ~27x forward P/E versus about 17-18x for Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman, but most analysts (24 covering, consensus Buy, $228.83 average target) do not call it overvalued.

simple.evidence: RTX has three clear segments (Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney, Raytheon) selling aircraft parts, engines and weapons, which a careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Sales grew every year from $56,587M (2020) to $88,603M (2025), but earnings were volatile, including a 2020 net loss and the 2023 GTF charge.

integrity.evidence: Management is candid in guidance and has returned cash via dividends and buybacks, but RTX settled bribery and defective-pricing cases with the DOJ and SEC in 2024, and pay is tied mainly to EPS and free cash flow.

b6.evidence: Calio has divested non-core units (e.g., Collins actuation to Safran) to focus the portfolio, but RTX itself is the product of large mergers (UTC-Rockwell Collins 2018, UTC-Raytheon 2020).

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 9.4% (stockanalysis, TTM), held down by $53.3B of goodwill from mergers, with $37.4B of debt.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow of $7,940M exceeded net income of $6,732M, and 2026 guidance is $8.5-8.75B.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings have been absorbed by mergers, spin-offs (Carrier, Otis) and GTF costs, making the value created per retained dollar hard to measure.

safety.evidence: At $186.47 the stock trades at about 32x trailing GAAP EPS and a Nash-style DCF gives roughly $59 per share, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E near 25 for adjusted EPS growth around 15% and ~9% revenue growth is full but not extreme for a business with a $289B backlog.

mu5.evidence: Failure risk is low given diversified, long-lived franchises, but program risks (GTF recall, fixed-price charges), budget politics and leverage are real ways to stumble.

reinvest.evidence: RTX can reinvest in capacity and new programs for decades given its backlog, but at returns around 9-10% on capital rather than high returns.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with a simple story: growing defense budgets and air travel plus fading GTF charges should lift earnings.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 32 (forward ~25) is well above EPS growth of about 15% guided for 2026.

runway.evidence: A record $289B backlog and new programs (LTAMDS, SPY-6, GTF Advantage, counter-drone) support years of mid-to-high single-digit growth, but not explosive expansion.

ly7.evidence: Insiders sold shares in 2026 (e.g., an EVP sold 13,655 shares in August at about $224) and diluted shares rose from 1,343.6M (2024) to 1,365.0M (Q2 2026).

ly8.evidence: RTX is a $250B mega-cap followed by about 24 analysts and widely owned by institutions.

fi2.evidence: RTX keeps refreshing its portfolio with GTF Advantage, LTAMDS, SPY-6, hypersonic and counter-drone systems as older products mature.

fi3.evidence: Its company-funded R&D ($2,807M in 2025) plus customer-funded development yields fielded systems and major wins such as the $22.9B Tomahawk contract in August 2026.

fi4.evidence: Its global sales network wins large foreign military sales (Patriot buyers across Europe and the Middle East), but much defense demand comes through government procurement rather than sales skill.

longterm.evidence: It invests for long programs and capacity, but management is focused on near-term EPS and free-cash-flow targets and shareholder returns.

gr1.evidence: RTX had $88,603M of 2025 sales and a market cap of about $251B.

ni10.evidence: RTX reported a net loss of $3,519M attributable to common shareowners in 2020.

gr4.evidence: RTX (as successor to United Technologies) has paid a dividend every year for decades, currently $2.92 a year annualized.

eps10.evidence: The 2020 UTC-Raytheon merger and spin-offs of Carrier and Otis make ten-year EPS comparisons inconsistent; GAAP diluted EPS was $4.96 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: The price of $186.47 is about 52 times average 2023-2025 diluted EPS of $3.58.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 32.2 times P/B of about 3.72 is roughly 120, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its products are leading but not ten times better than rivals; e.g., the GTF competes closely with the CFM LEAP.

timing.evidence: Rising defense budgets, depleted munitions stocks after Ukraine and Middle East conflicts, and strong air-travel demand favor RTX now, with Q2 2026 organic sales up 16%.

th3.evidence: RTX is a consolidated incumbent built from century-old businesses, not a company that started by dominating a small market.

team.evidence: The management team is experienced and executing well, but it is a professional team rather than an exceptional founder.

th5.evidence: RTX has entrenched channels with the Pentagon, allied governments, Airbus, Boeing and airlines, plus a global aftermarket network.

durable.evidence: Engines and missiles have 30+ year program lives, certification barriers and sole-source positions such as the F135, so its position should largely hold for 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its opportunities (missile defense, engines) are well known and contested by major rivals.

trend.evidence: It is a leading beneficiary of the global rearmament and air-defense trend and air-travel growth, but not of a technology platform shift like AI or cloud.

dr1.evidence: Adjusted EPS grew 21% year over year in Q1 and Q2 2026, and guidance was raised from $6.60-6.80 to $7.10-7.25.

dr2.evidence: GTF charges should fade and defense production ramps, but much of this is widely expected and priced in.

dr4.evidence: Defense spending is driven by geopolitics rather than rates, while lower rates help airline customers and its $37.4B debt; the economy matters mainly for commercial aerospace.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q3 2026 results on October 20, 2026, large munitions and Patriot orders, and GTF fleet recovery.

dr7.evidence: Moderate growth, a full valuation and program risk make it unsuited to a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was about 20% in 2025 ($17,789M on $88,603M sales).

fcfyield.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow of $7,940M is about a 3.2% yield on a ~$251B market cap (about 4.5% on trailing-twelve-month FCF), fair for mid-single to high-single-digit growth.

gb2.evidence: FY2025 operating profit of $9,300M is only about 3.3% of an enterprise value near $282B.

pa2.evidence: The GTF powder-metal recall was a temporary, fixable setback, but it is largely resolved and the stock no longer trades at distressed levels.

pa4.evidence: Entrenched franchises, a $289B backlog and government customers make permanent capital loss unlikely, though overpaying is a risk.

wo1.evidence: RTX is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Engine and missile production costs are not falling rapidly with volume; supply constraints have raised costs.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable markets grow steadily, not many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: Defense revenue is insulated from commodities and rates, but commercial aerospace is exposed to airline cycles, fuel prices and metals and tariff costs.

ns1.evidence: RTX raises aftermarket parts prices rather than passing scale savings back to customers.

ns4.evidence: Rising defense spend and a growing installed GTF fleet should strengthen its position, but new low-cost entrants and GTF reputation issues cloud the picture.

va2.evidence: It solves large, painful problems: defending against missiles and drones and powering safe, fuel-efficient air travel.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the secular rearmament and air-defense trend, but as an old business adapting rather than one built for the trend.

tn2.evidence: The market sees RTX as a defense and aerospace prime, which is what it is; no large gap between story and reality.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company outside small caps, China, commodities, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year 2020-2025 and it is profitable ($6,732M 2025 net income), though debt of $37,383M exceeds cash of $8,305M.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in each recent quarter (e.g., $3,195M Q4 2025, $1,309M Q1 2026, $2,878M Q2 2026), but debt exceeded cash every quarter.

tn6.evidence: FY2025 revenue grew 9.7%, and 2026 is tracking around 10-12% (Q2 2026 sales $24,708M, 16% organic growth).

tn7.evidence: FY2025 revenue growth of 9.7% plus FCF margin of 9.0% is about 18.7, well under 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 9.7% while cost of sales rose 8.4% and R&D fell, so operating profit rose from $6,538M to $9,300M.

tn9.evidence: It fails instant kills: debt ($37,383M) exceeds cash ($8,305M) and operating margin (~10.5% in 2025) is below 20%.

tn10.evidence: RTX faces ongoing GTF-related litigation and export-control and contract-pricing scrutiny, though its major 2024 DOJ/SEC cases are settled.

tn11.evidence: RTX provides engines, aircraft systems and missile-defense weapons that help airlines and governments fly safely and defend themselves, charging per unit plus long-term aftermarket and sustainment contracts.

tn13.evidence: Total 80: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5, operating margin 5, short interest (1.1%) 10, institutional ownership (~81%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 (stock roughly doubled) 10, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture/mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year but operating margin dipped in 2023, FCF fell in 2022 and 2024, and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is 5.3x ($9,300M/$1,749M), current ratio 1.03 and liabilities 1.55x equity pass, but assets excluding goodwill ($117,736M) are only 1.13x liabilities ($103,941M).

tn18.evidence: Calio has executed well since 2024, but he has been CEO for about two years, is not a founder, and has no notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: RTX beat adjusted EPS estimates in recent quarters, e.g., Q2 2026 $1.89 vs about $1.66 expected.

tn21.evidence: No fraud or auditor issues, but past legal settlements, the merger-built structure and insider selling during the 2026 run-up are yellow flags.

tn22.evidence: RTX has $88.6B of revenue, solid profits and does not rely on share sales or hype.

tn24.evidence: A ~3-4.5% FCF yield implies mid-to-high single-digit long-term growth, roughly in line with the ~10% revenue growth RTX is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using 9.9% average growth, 7.5% average FCF margin, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate gives about $59 per share versus $186.47.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 25 is above defense peers (Lockheed ~17x, Northrop ~18x) and the PEG is about 2.3.
